cards.text: This is the burden Habakkuk the prophet received in a vision. And it doesn't open with a polite little prayer, friend. Habakkuk opens by crying out to the LORD, and he's got QUESTIONS.

cards.question: What's the first thing Habakkuk asks the LORD?

answers.text: How long must I call for help
Why did You choose me for this
Where should I go to speak next

cards.question: True or false: Habakkuk says he cries out to the LORD, "Violence!" but the LORD does not save.

cards.text: I know waiting on help: in the junk drawer, every time it opened I thought THIS IS IT, and it was somebody looking for TAPE. And Habakkuk says destruction and violence are right in front of him, with strife and conflict everywhere.

cards.question: Habakkuk asks the LORD why He makes him see iniquity. Then he asks, Why do You tolerate ___?

cards.text: Because of it all, Habakkuk says the law is paralyzed and justice never goes forth. PARALYZED, like a cookie stamper in the back of a drawer: still there, just not doing ANYTHING.

cards.question: Habakkuk says the wicked hem in the righteous. What happens to justice?

cards.text: Now the LORD answers: "Look at the nations and observe—be utterly astounded!" Not mildly surprised, not "huh, neat," but UTTERLY astounded.

cards.question: The LORD says He is doing a work in your days. How hard will it be to believe?

answers.text: You would never believe it even if told
Only the wise will understand it at first
Everyone will see it coming from far away

cards.text: So what's this unbelievable work? The LORD says He is raising up a nation.

cards.question: Which nation does the LORD say He is raising up?

cards.text: The Chaldeans, a people from Babylon (Jeremiah 50:1). The LORD calls them that ruthless and impetuous nation, and they march through the breadth of the earth.

cards.question: Why do the Chaldeans march through the breadth of the earth?

answers.text: To take homes that belong to others
To take back land they once owned
To hunt down one rival king

cards.text: Taking homes that aren't theirs, like the coworker who borrows your chair for ONE meeting and three weeks later it's HIS chair. The LORD says they are dreaded and feared.

cards.question: True or false: The Chaldeans get their idea of justice from themselves.

cards.text: Then the LORD describes their army, starting with the horses. He compares them to leopards and to wolves of the night.

cards.question: Leopards and wolves of the night. What do those pictures say about the Chaldean army?

cards.text: Swifter than leopards, fiercer than wolves, friend. Their horsemen charge ahead, and their cavalry comes from afar.

cards.question: The LORD says the Chaldeans fly like a vulture. What is that vulture doing?

cards.text: All of them come bent on violence, their hordes advancing like the east wind. That word again, friend: violence.

cards.question: The LORD says the Chaldeans gather prisoners like sand. What's that picture saying?

answers.text: More prisoners than anyone could count
Their prisoners slip right through their hands
Their prisoners are left out in the desert

cards.question: The Chaldeans scoff at kings and make rulers an object of scorn. True or false: A strong fortress makes them turn back.

cards.text: They LAUGH at every fortress and build up siege ramps to seize it. Then they sweep by like the wind and pass through, and those walls lasted about as long as my willpower next to a fresh tray of cookies.

cards.question: The LORD says the Chaldeans are guilty. Their own ___ is their god.

cards.text: We'll stop the oven timer right here for now. Stick with me, friend, because Habakkuk and the LORD are just getting started.

findings.problem: In a prophetic passage, this card asks the baker to pick the wording of Habakkuk's opening line ('How long must I call for help' versus other possible first questions). It tests which words come first, not the movement or meaning of the complaint. Card 1 only says he cries out with questions, so 'Why did You choose me for this' is just as easy to reason toward.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says. Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'It gets bought' is close to the right answer 'It gets perverted'. Bought justice is a kind of perverted justice, so a baker could argue it is right.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Habakkuk 1:8 compares the Chaldeans' horses to leopards and wolves of the night, and card 7 says so. The question then applies the comparison to 'the Chaldean army' and answers 'It is fast and fierce,' which widens what the text compares.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The last story card is only the 'story isn't over' line and tells no verse, but it cites Habakkuk 1:11. Every story card is supposed to cite the verses it tells. This card tells none, and the JSON still needs a verses value.
findings.question: When the last story card is only the 'story isn't over' line, what should its verses field cite? The last verse of the passage, the last verse of the stop, or something else?
